statement: Win32 calls are declared as a group of external function signatures that run nothing themselves; each runs only when a policy-loading, privilege or system-info routine calls it. Registry access goes through .NET registry classes, not declarations.

evidence.shows: One class only declares native functions from advapi32, userenv, user32 and kernel32
A routine that calls those declarations to enable a privilege
Opening and closing a policy source calls the hive load and unload functions

statement: Nothing in the project changes which Windows API code exists: all native declarations are compiled unconditionally. Only the Debug/Release build settings differ, and they do not touch registry or Win32 use.

assumed.why: Conditional compilation symbols beyond Debug and Trace were not found, but a full search of every build input was not made.
assumed.ifWrong: A build variant could add or remove registry code.

evidence.shows: Debug and Release configurations set only debug and trace flags
Declarations carry no conditional compilation

statement: The contract with Windows is by name: native functions are named with their DLL (for example RegLoadKeyW in advapi32), and registry locations are text paths such as Software\Policies under the machine or user root. Roots accepted by text are HKCU, HKU and HKLM, short or long form.

evidence.shows: Hive load and unload declared with DLL name and wide-string arguments
Typed registry path is split at the first backslash and its root name matched
Policy locations are three fixed lowercase registry branches

statement: Windows APIs are not tied to screens except one: the main window hides its horizontal scrollbar through a user32 call. Screens otherwise reach the registry only indirectly, by asking a policy loader to open, save or close a source.

evidence.shows: Main window calls ShowScrollBar on the setting info panel
Dialog builds policy loaders for registry, file, user GPO and hive choices

statement: Per-user state lives in the current user's registry under Software\Policy Plus: last policy source types and paths, ADMX folder, language, and acknowledgement flags. It is read at start and written when sources change; no session exists. Failure to create the key silently falls back to defaults.

evidence.shows: Settings class wraps a registry key and ignores creation failure
Key Software\Policy Plus opened and last sources read
Source types and data saved back

statement: Registry data is shaped in code: policy values are typed numeric, string, multi-string or binary and passed through one policy-source interface, with registry, policy file and hive-file implementations. Unsigned 32/64-bit numbers are converted to the registry's signed form on write and back on read; native structs are defined for token privileges.

evidence.shows: Single interface for reading and writing policy values
Registry proxy reinterprets signed and unsigned numbers
Two native structures for privilege adjustment

statement: Windows needs no configured address: its places are fixed in code. Policy files sit under the system root GroupPolicy and GroupPolicyUsers folders; the registry roots come from user choice or the saved settings. The only outside address, the ADMX installer download, is a constant.

evidence.shows: Local policy file and version file paths built from the system root
Per-user policy paths built from a typed SID
Microsoft MSI address is a constant in code

statement: The program calls Windows itself for its core behaviour: advapi32 loads and unloads a user registry hive and adjusts process privileges; userenv refreshes Group Policy; user32 broadcasts a setting-change message and hides a scrollbar; kernel32 reads the Windows edition. Edition decides whether Windows applies policy or the program writes the registry itself.

evidence.shows: All native functions called, by DLL
Edition code is looked up in a list of editions having Group Policy
Policy refresh is called, or registry diff written and change broadcast

statement: The ADMX download fetches an installer package over the network and runs it with msiexec with no signature, hash or publisher check, then moves its files into the policy folder, taking ownership of it when running as administrator.

evidence.shows: Fixed download address
File downloaded and run through msiexec with no verification
Administrator takes ownership of destination folder

statement: The typed SID for a user policy source is joined straight into a file path under the system folder, then written to, with no check of its form, so a crafted value could point the write elsewhere.

evidence.shows: Argument concatenated into GroupPolicyUsers path
Argument comes from a text box

statement: Results of privilege enabling and of hive loading are ignored: if the privilege or the hive load fails, the program proceeds without saying why, and a later save can fail or be silently skipped.

evidence.shows: Return values of native privilege calls are not checked
Hive load result ignored; failure only noticed as a missing key

statement: The policy-version file is rewritten in place after being read, so a failure midway leaves it truncated; Windows may then not notice the policy change.

evidence.shows: File lines read, then file reopened for overwrite and rewritten line by line

statement: Permissions are not declared in data or code by the system: the executable manifest asks Windows for the highest rights the user holds, and code then turns on backup, restore and take-ownership privileges when needed. Other checks are write probes against the real target.

evidence.shows: Project embeds an application manifest, which sets the execution level to highest available
Privilege is enabled by adjusting the process token
Writability is tested by writing and deleting a probe value
Administrator role is checked from the Windows identity

statement: Three screen-level uses of Windows APIs exist: the main window hides its horizontal scrollbar through a user32 call, the main window's load asks kernel32 (via the edition check) whether Group Policy exists, and the ADMX download dialog enables token privileges through advapi32. Everything else reaches the registry only indirectly, by asking a policy loader to open, save or close a source.

evidence.shows: Main window calls ShowScrollBar on the setting info panel
Main window load calls HasGroupPolicyInfrastructure
That check reads the Windows edition through kernel32
Download dialog enables take-ownership and restore privileges
Dialog builds policy loaders for registry, file, user GPO and hive choices

statement: The contract with Windows is by name: native functions are named with their DLL (for example RegLoadKeyW in advapi32), and registry locations are text paths such as Software\Policies under the machine or user root. Roots accepted by text are HKCU, HKU and HKLM, short or long form. Three lowercase branches (software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies, system\currentcontrolset\policies) are fixed in code, but only to scope which keys a policy-file difference tracks; other registry paths are still readable and writable.

evidence.shows: Hive load and unload declared with DLL name and wide-string arguments
Typed registry path is split at the first backslash and its root name matched
PolicyKeys lists the three branches, which only limit what ApplyDifference tracks

statement: Registry data is shaped in code: policy values are typed numeric, string, multi-string or binary and passed through one policy-source interface, with registry, policy file and hive-file implementations. The registry implementation converts unsigned 32/64-bit numbers to the registry's signed form on write and back on read; native structs are defined for token privileges.

evidence.shows: Single interface for reading and writing policy values
RegistryPolicyProxy.SetValue reinterprets unsigned numbers as signed before writing
GetValue reinterprets signed numbers back to unsigned
Two native structures for privilege adjustment

statement: Nothing in the project changes which Windows API code exists: all native declarations are compiled unconditionally in every build. The only conditional compilation is the generated _MyType check in the settings designer; no #If or #Const touches registry or Win32 code, and the project defines no custom constants. Debug and Release differ only in debug, trace and optimisation flags, and the manifest is embedded in all builds.

evidence.shows: Debug and Release set only debug, trace, optimisation and output flags, no custom constants
The only #If in the source is this generated _MyType check (also line 43)
Application manifest is set unconditionally
Declarations carry no conditional compilation

statement: When the user presses start, the ADMX download fetches a Microsoft installer package from a fixed https address with WebClient, with no hash, signature or publisher check, and the app allows TLS 1.0 and 1.1 as well as 1.2 for it. It is unpacked with msiexec /a (an administrative extract, not an install) and only the ADMX/ADML files are moved into the policy folder the app takes ownership of as administrator. A tampered package, for example through a downgraded connection, would put attacker-chosen policy definition files there; reach is this download only.

evidence.shows: Fixed https download address on a Microsoft host
SecurityProtocol set to Tls, Tls11 and Tls12 at main window load
Whole download runs only from the start button click
Package downloaded and extracted with msiexec /a, no verification
Administrator takes ownership of the destination, then extracted files are moved in
